lesson.text: Quick memory: how do you find the price of one apple in a pack of 4 that costs 2 gold? (Share it: 0.50 gold each.) Adverts want you to buy without working things out. Today: how adverts persuade.
An advert is a message paid for by someone who wants you to buy something or do something. Adverts are on screens, in videos and games, on buses, on posters and in shops.
Adverts use tricks: catchy songs you can't forget, bright colours, happy people having fun, and words like 'amazing', 'new!' and 'the best'.

'Ends soon!' and 'Nearly sold out!' try to make you rush. 'Everyone has one!' makes you feel left out. A price of 9.99 looks much less than 10, but 10 − 9.99 = 0.01: one hundredth of a gold coin less.
Some people online are paid to show things in their videos. They should say it is an advert. Ask: are they telling me because they love it, or because they were paid?
Friends can make us want things too: when everyone in your group has something, you may feel you must have it. Ask: do I really want it, or do I want to fit in? Real friends like you for you.
Check an advert with questions: Who made it? What do they want me to do? What does it not tell me? How will I feel about it in a week? What else could I do with the gold?
Try it in the world: make an honest advert on a sign for something you built, with no tricks, just true facts. Next: ways to pay.

exercises.hint: Who pays for an advert, and why?
choices: to make you want to buy or do something
to tell you the whole truth
exercises.explain: Adverts are paid for by people who want you to buy or do something.

exercises.prompt: Adverts always tell you about a thing's problems.
exercises.hint: Would a seller point out the bad parts?
exercises.explain: False: adverts show the good side and often leave the problems out.

exercises.prompt: An advert says 'Everyone has one!' How does it want you to feel?
exercises.hint: Think about fitting in with a group.
choices: left out if you don't buy it
exercises.explain: It wants you to feel left out, so that you buy it to fit in.

exercises.hint: Look around a town, or at a screen.
choices: on screens, in games, on buses and in shops
exercises.explain: Adverts are everywhere: screens, videos, games, buses, posters and shops.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a fact, or persuasion?
exercises.hint: Can you check it with a ruler, a scale or a price tag?
exercises.explain: Facts can be checked: the price, what it is made of, its weight. Persuasion is words meant to make you want it.

exercises.prompt: Match each trick to what it tries to do.
exercises.hint: Think about how each one makes you feel or think.
exercises.explain: 'Ends soon!' makes you rush; a song sticks in your head; 'Everyone has one!' makes you feel left out; 9.99 looks cheaper than 10.

exercises.prompt: A price is 9.99 gold instead of 10 gold. How much less is it, in gold?
exercises.explain: 10 − 9.99 = 0.01 gold: just one hundredth of a coin.

exercises.prompt: A video star shows a toy and says 'I love it!' What should you ask?
choices: were they paid to show it?
exercises.explain: Ask if they were paid. Paid posts should say that they are adverts.

exercises.prompt: Friends having something can make you want it too.
exercises.explain: True: that is why it helps to ask, 'Do I really want it, or do I want to fit in?'

exercises.prompt: An advert says 'Buy 2, get 1 free!' but you need only one. Is it a good deal for you?
exercises.hint: Work out what you would really pay for what you need.
choices: no: you would pay for 2 but need only 1
yes: free things are always good
exercises.explain: Paying for 2 when you need 1 costs more, even with a free one. A deal only helps if you need that many.

exercises.prompt: Which question helps you check an advert?
choices: What does it not tell me?
exercises.explain: Asking what it does not tell you (the full price, the problems, how long it lasts) helps you decide.

exercises.prompt: All Bram's friends have a new hat, and he feels he must have one. What could he ask himself?
exercises.hint: Remember the advert trick 'Everyone has one!'.
choices: do I really want it, or want to fit in?
how fast can I buy it?
exercises.explain: Asking whether he really wants it, or just wants to fit in, helps him choose for himself. Real friends like him for him.

exercises.prompt: A 'sale' price is always a good deal.
exercises.hint: Is it a good deal if you didn't need it?
exercises.explain: False: a sale saves money only on things you really need or want; otherwise it is money spent.

exercises.prompt: Kites cost 5 gold each. The advert says 'Buy 2, get 1 free!' How much do 3 kites cost?
exercises.explain: You pay for 2 kites: 2 × 5 = 10 gold for 3 kites.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: an advert, or not an advert?
items: a paid video showing a toy
exercises.hint: Did someone pay for it to make you buy or do something?
exercises.explain: Adverts: the trainers poster, the paid toy video and the sponsored result were all paid for. Not adverts: the weather, the frog book and the news inform you.
